presentingComplaint: Several months of progressive fatigue, poor appetite, itching and bilateral ankle swelling.
history: 58-year-old man with a 12-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes and hypertension presents with insidious, months-long fatigue, anorexia, nausea, generalised pruritus, nocturia and gradually worsening bilateral leg oedema. No dysuria, haematuria, colicky flank pain or recent illness. On amlodipine and an ACE inhibitor; NSAIDs used intermittently for knee pain. Long-standing microalbuminuria noted at prior reviews but no structured follow-up. No acute fluid loss, sepsis or nephrotoxin binge to suggest an abrupt insult.
examination: Pale, mildly uraemic-looking, well perfused. Bilateral pitting pedal oedema to mid-shin. BP elevated. Chest clear, no gallop; JVP mildly raised. Abdomen soft, no bruit, no palpable bladder or pulsatile mass. No asterixis, no pericardial rub, no focal neurology. No rash. Fundi show hypertensive/diabetic changes.

labs.urinalysis: proteinuria, no active sediment, no casts

imaging: Renal ultrasound: bilaterally small (right 8.4 cm, left 8.7 cm) echogenic kidneys with cortical thinning and loss of corticomedullary differentiation; no hydronephrosis or obstructing calculus. Confirms chronic, irreversible parenchymal disease.
differentialDiagnoses: Acute kidney injury superimposed on CKD
finalDiagnosis: Chronic kidney disease, stage G4A3 (diabetic and hypertensive nephropathy)
citations: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of CKD 2024
contraindications: Avoid nephrotoxic NSAIDs and iodinated contrast where possible
Renally dose all drugs to eGFR; hold/adjust metformin at eGFR <30
ACE inhibitor: monitor K+ and creatinine; hyperkalaemia risk at 5.4 mmol/L
edgeCases: Superimposed AKI (e.g., NSAID or contrast insult) can acutely worsen a chronic baseline and be missed if prior creatinine not sought
Normal-sized or large kidneys despite advanced CKD point to diabetic nephropathy, amyloid, HIV nephropathy or polycystic disease rather than typical shrunken kidneys
expectedMaiK: Bilaterally small echogenic kidneys, stable elevation of creatinine over >14 months, anaemia and CKD-mineral-bone disease indicate chronic rather than acute kidney disease; management centres on slowing progression (BP and glycaemic control, RAAS blockade with K+ monitoring, SGLT2 inhibitor) and treating complications, not on a reversible acute insult.
expectedNextQuestions: Is there an earlier creatinine/eGFR to confirm chronicity and rate of decline?
Any NSAID, contrast or nephrotoxin exposure, or symptoms of obstruction?
expectedInvestigations: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and urine microscopy for casts
Renal ultrasound for kidney size and to exclude obstruction
CKD complication panel: potassium, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate, PTH, haemoglobin

investigations: serum potassium, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate and PTH
